claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 begins in a high-temperature single-phase BCC state.
The variety of phases formed during cooling and aging is driven by diffusion-mediated local segregation during slow cooling.
Al is a particularly important segregating component in this alloy.
Compositional partitioning promotes nucleation of secondary ordered phases within the BCC matrix during subsequent thermal aging.
Slow cooling allows more atomic segregation than rapid quenching.
Local Al-enriched or otherwise segregated regions form within the BCC matrix.
Segregated regions act as nucleation sites for ordered or secondary-phase precipitates.
Differential elemental diffusion rates during slow cooling produce elemental segregation.
Segregation and the resulting compositional gradients destabilize the homogeneous BCC phase.
Compositional gradients accelerate secondary-phase nucleation and growth during thermal aging.
Rapid quenching minimizes segregation and therefore favors retention of metastable BCC structure.
After identical aging, slowly cooled specimens will contain more secondary ordered phases than rapidly quenched specimens.
Rapidly quenched and aged specimens will largely retain the BCC phase.
The predicted phase differences will be detectable by XRD and electron microscopy.
The mechanism requires cooling and aging conditions under which diffusion is sufficiently active for significant segregation and phase nucleation.
The mechanism should not manifest under extremely rapid cooling or at aging temperatures too low for appreciable diffusion.
The high-temperature BCC baseline has minimal compositional segregation and no significant secondary-phase formation.
Stress-induced transformations or other dominant kinetic factors could invalidate the proposed segregation-controlled mechanism.
The individual elemental diffusion rates in this multicomponent alloy are not fully quantified.
